fixes.answer: Life was noticeably slower and, in some ways, more present. People were less [[contactable]] and more likely to be fully engaged in their [[immediate surroundings]] rather than staring at a screen. Getting lost, being bored or having to memorise information were normal. While we have gained incredible convenience, I think we have lost a certain patience and the ability to simply be [[idle]], which had its own value.
fixes.why: 'patience' and 'value' are plain; marked 'contactable' and 'immediate surroundings'

fixes.answer: The effects can be quite detrimental. Excessive use seems to be linked to reduced [[attention spans]], disrupted sleep and increased anxiety, partly due to the constant stream of notifications. It can also erode face-to-face social skills and lead to a [[sedentary]] lifestyle. There is even a recognised phenomenon of phone addiction. So while occasional use is harmless, overuse can genuinely [[impair]] both our mental and physical wellbeing.
fixes.why: 'addiction' and 'wellbeing' are plain; marked 'attention spans' and 'sedentary'; softened the health claim

fixes.answer: They have transformed them in mixed ways. On one hand, they let us maintain connections effortlessly across distances. On the other, they often [[intrude]] on our real-world interactions; it is common to see people together physically but absorbed in their phones. This phenomenon, sometimes called [[phubbing]], can make people feel ignored. So smartphones have expanded our virtual social lives while sometimes [[diminishing]] the quality of our present ones.

I anticipate devices will become even more integrated into our lives, perhaps evolving beyond the handheld phone into [[wearables]] or augmented reality glasses. Artificial intelligence will make them ever more [[anticipatory]] and personalised. The line between the digital and physical worlds is likely to [[blur]] further. While this promises even greater convenience, I hope it comes with a stronger awareness of the need to remain present and in control.

There are several practical strategies. Turning off non-essential notifications immediately reduces the constant pull to check the phone. [[Designating]] device-free times and zones, such as during meals or in the bedroom, helps re-establish boundaries. Using apps that track and limit screen time can raise awareness of usage. Ultimately, consciously replacing [[mindless scrolling]] with more rewarding activities is the most sustainable way to [[loosen the phone's grip]].
fixes.why: 'replacing' and 'rewarding' are plain; marked 'designating', 'mindless scrolling', and the full idiom 'loosen the phone's grip'

fixes.answer: The advantages include safety, as parents can stay in contact, and access to educational resources. It also helps children develop digital literacy. However, the disadvantages are considerable: exposure to inappropriate content, [[cyberbullying]], addiction and reduced physical activity. It can also [[hinder]] the development of face-to-face social skills. So while there are benefits, I believe children's phone use needs careful [[supervision]] and sensible limits.

I think that is an exaggeration, but it contains an [[uncomfortable truth]]. Obviously, people survived perfectly well before phones, so it is not a literal dependency. However, phones have become so [[integral]] to how we work, navigate and communicate that living without one would be genuinely inconvenient and isolating in modern society. So while we could live without them, our society has become so [[reliant]] on them that it would be a difficult adjustment.
